title: B+ Tree Indexes
text:
A B+ tree is a balanced search tree used by most relational databases to index table columns. All records live in the leaf level, and the leaves are linked together, which makes range scans efficient: the engine finds the first key and then walks the linked leaves. Internal nodes only store separator keys, so each node fits many keys and the tree stays shallow, typically three or four levels even for millions of rows.

Because the tree is ordered, a B+ tree index supports equality lookups, range predicates such as BETWEEN, and ORDER BY without an extra sort. Composite indexes follow the leftmost-prefix rule: an index on (a, b) helps queries filtering on a, or on a and b, but not on b alone.

title: Hash Indexes
text:
A hash index applies a hash function to the key and stores a pointer in the matching bucket. Point lookups by exact key are close to constant time, which is faster than walking a tree.

The trade-off is that hashing destroys ordering. A hash index cannot answer range queries, prefix matches or ORDER BY, and it is useless for inequality predicates. PostgreSQL supports hash indexes for equality-only access patterns such as looking up a session by token.

title: Multiversion Concurrency Control
text:
MVCC lets readers and writers work at the same time without blocking each other. Instead of overwriting a row in place, an update creates a new version, and each transaction sees a consistent snapshot of the data as of when it started.

Because old versions are kept, a long-running report does not block updates, and updates do not block the report. The cost is storage for old row versions, which must be cleaned up later; in PostgreSQL this cleanup is done by VACUUM.

title: Two-Phase Locking
text:
Two-phase locking (2PL) is a concurrency-control protocol that guarantees conflict-serializable schedules. A transaction has a growing phase in which it may acquire locks but not release them, followed by a shrinking phase in which it releases locks and may not acquire new ones.

Strict 2PL holds all exclusive locks until commit, which also prevents cascading aborts. The downside of locking protocols is the possibility of deadlock, where two transactions each wait for a lock held by the other; databases detect the cycle in a wait-for graph and abort one victim.

title: Write-Ahead Logging
text:
Write-ahead logging is how databases survive crashes. Before a change to a data page is written to disk, a log record describing the change must first be flushed to durable storage. Commit only returns once the commit record is in the log.

After a crash, recovery replays the log: committed changes that never reached the data files are redone, and changes from transactions that never committed are undone. Periodic checkpoints bound how much log must be replayed, keeping restart time short.

title: Atomic Counters in Redis
text:
Redis executes commands on a single thread, so each individual command is atomic. DECR and INCR change a counter and return the new value in one step, with no window in which two clients can read the same stale value.

This makes Redis a common choice for inventory counters in flash sales: each buyer runs DECR on the stock key, and if the returned value is negative the purchase is rejected and the counter is incremented back. For multi-step logic, a Lua script runs atomically on the server as well.

title: Optimistic Concurrency Control
text:
Optimistic concurrency assumes conflicts are rare. A transaction reads a row together with its version number, does its work without holding locks, and then updates with a condition such as WHERE id = 7 AND version = 3, incrementing the version.

If another transaction changed the row in between, the update matches zero rows and the application retries. This avoids lock waits under low contention, but under heavy contention, such as thousands of buyers hitting the same product, retries pile up and throughput collapses.

title: The CAP Theorem
text:
The CAP theorem states that when a network partition happens, a distributed data store must choose between consistency and availability. A consistent system refuses some requests so that every read sees the latest write; an available system keeps answering but may return stale data.

Since partitions cannot be ruled out in real networks, the practical choice is between CP systems, which favour correctness, and AP systems, which favour uptime and reconcile later.

title: Consistent Hashing
text:
Consistent hashing maps both servers and keys onto the same ring of hash values. Each key belongs to the first server found clockwise from it.

When a server is added or removed, only the keys in its neighbouring arc move, instead of almost every key moving as with hash mod N. Virtual nodes, where each physical server appears many times on the ring, smooth out the load. Distributed caches and databases such as Cassandra and DynamoDB use this idea to rebalance data.

title: Kubernetes Horizontal Pod Autoscaler
text:
The Horizontal Pod Autoscaler changes the number of pod replicas in a Deployment based on observed metrics, most commonly CPU utilisation relative to the pod's CPU request. If average utilisation is above the target, it adds replicas; if below, it removes them, within configured minimum and maximum bounds.

The HPA reads metrics from metrics-server. If containers have no CPU requests, utilisation cannot be computed and the autoscaler shows unknown targets and never scales.

title: Predictive Alerting with PromQL
text:
Prometheus' predict_linear function fits a straight line to a time series over a window and extrapolates it into the future. A classic use is predicting disk exhaustion: predict_linear(node_filesystem_avail_bytes[6h], 4 * 3600) < 0 fires if free space is on track to hit zero within four hours.

This warns operators before the problem happens rather than after the disk is already full, which a static threshold like 'free space below 10%' cannot do.

title: The TLS Handshake
text:
TLS secures HTTPS connections. During the handshake the client and server agree on a protocol version and cipher suite, the server presents its certificate so the client can verify its identity against a trusted certificate authority, and both sides derive shared session keys, usually through an ephemeral Diffie-Hellman exchange.

TLS 1.3 cut the handshake to a single round trip and removed older insecure ciphers. Certificates expire, so automated renewal, for example with Let's Encrypt and Certbot, is standard practice.

title: BM25 Ranking
text:
BM25 is a keyword ranking function used by search engines. A document scores higher when it contains the query terms often, but term frequency saturates, so the tenth occurrence adds much less than the first. Rare terms count for more than common ones through inverse document frequency, and long documents are normalised so they do not win just by being long.

BM25 is strong at exact matches such as error codes, identifiers and names, but it has no notion of synonyms or meaning.

title: Retrieval-Augmented Generation
text:
Retrieval-augmented generation grounds a language model's answer in external documents. The documents are split into chunks and indexed; at question time the most relevant chunks are retrieved and placed into the prompt, and the model is instructed to answer from them and cite them.

RAG reduces hallucination and lets a model use private or up-to-date information without retraining. Its quality is limited by retrieval: if the right chunk is not retrieved, the model cannot use it, which is why chunking strategy and retriever choice matter so much.

title: Two-Phase Commit
text:
Two-phase commit coordinates a transaction that spans several databases or services. In the prepare phase the coordinator asks every participant whether it can commit; each one writes its changes durably and votes yes or no. In the commit phase, if all voted yes, the coordinator tells everyone to commit, otherwise everyone rolls back.

The weakness is blocking: if the coordinator crashes after participants voted yes, they must hold their locks until it comes back, because they cannot decide alone.

title: Database Replication
text:
Replication keeps copies of a database on several servers. In PostgreSQL streaming replication the primary sends its write-ahead log to standby servers, which replay it to stay up to date. Standbys can serve read-only queries and can be promoted if the primary fails.

Asynchronous replication is fast but a failover can lose the last few transactions; synchronous replication waits for a standby to confirm, trading latency for durability.

title: Rate Limiting with Redis
text:
A rate limiter caps how many requests a client may make in a time window. A simple fixed-window limiter in Redis runs INCR on a key such as rate:user42:202610281530 and sets an expiry on first use; if the counter exceeds the limit, the request is rejected with HTTP 429.

Sliding-window and token-bucket variants smooth out the burst that fixed windows allow at window boundaries.

title: Transaction Isolation Levels
text:
SQL defines isolation levels by which anomalies they allow. Read Uncommitted permits dirty reads of uncommitted data. Read Committed prevents dirty reads but allows non-repeatable reads, where the same row changes between two reads. Repeatable Read keeps rows stable but may still show phantoms, new rows appearing in a range. Serializable prevents all of these and behaves as if transactions ran one at a time.

Higher isolation means fewer anomalies but more blocking or more aborted transactions.

title: Vector Search with Embeddings
text:
Embedding models turn text into dense vectors so that passages with similar meaning end up close together, even when they share no words. A query is embedded the same way and the nearest vectors are found by cosine similarity.

For large collections, exact search is replaced by approximate nearest-neighbour indexes such as HNSW, which trade a little accuracy for large speed-ups. Dense retrieval handles paraphrases well but can miss exact identifiers like error codes.

title: Load Balancing
text:
A load balancer spreads incoming requests across a pool of backend servers so no single server is overwhelmed. Common algorithms are round robin, least connections, and IP hash.

Health checks remove failing backends from the pool automatically. Nginx, HAProxy and cloud load balancers can work at layer 4 on TCP connections or at layer 7, where they can route on URL paths and headers.
